sentences.text: This part adds up most inputs with fixed weights, and daytime minutes count most: they raise a typical customer's chance of leaving steadily, from under 1% at 112 to about 17% at 249 minutes.

An international plan takes the chance from about 1% to about 16%, a voice-mail plan lowers it to under 1%, and more voice-mail messages raise it steadily, from about 1% at 0 to about 6% at 32 messages.

A higher international charge, more evening minutes (about 1% at 138 to about 3% at 266 minutes), a higher evening charge and more night-time minutes also raise it steadily, each by one to three points.

Through it, the state moves the chance from about 1% in most other states to about 6% in California and about 5% in Washington, and down to under 1% in Hawaii, Vermont and Colorado (41 to 80 training customers per state; the full list is in the technical detail).

This part combines customer-service calls with low daytime, evening and international use and acts on 3147 of 4000 training customers, 409 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, it changes the chance of leaving by less than a point.

Through it, daytime minutes lower the chance only while they stay below about 169 minutes (between 154 and 214 minutes for different customers), in an uneven way: for a typical customer, from about 47% at 91 minutes to about 1% at 352 minutes.

A higher international charge lowers it only while it stays below about 2.96 US dollars (between 2.96 and 4.53 US dollars for different customers), in an uneven way, from about 4% to about 1%, and a higher evening charge lowers it in an uneven way, from about 3% to about 1%.
Customer-service calls raise it in an uneven way, mostly for customers with an evening charge of 17.12 US dollars or less: from about 1% to about 6% between 0 and 3 calls, against no change above it.

This part reads the voice-mail plan and a few states: through it, a voice-mail plan lowers a typical customer's chance by less than a point, and customers in states other than Alabama, North Carolina and West Virginia get about 2% instead of about 1%.

Through this part, customer-service calls add nothing until about 4 calls, then raise the chance steadily; it acts on 306 of 4000 training customers, 154 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 16% without it and about 26% with it.
It is switched off for customers in West Virginia: for the typical customer it acts on, being in any other state takes the chance from about 16% to about 26%.
This part reads only the state and moves the chance by less than a point: up in Tennessee and Ohio, down in Nevada and California.

lead.text: For a typical customer (in West Virginia, area code 415, no international or voice-mail plan, 1 call to customer service and median usage) the model predicts a chance of leaving of about 1%; it adds up five parts: fixed-weight inputs, calls with low usage, a voice-mail discount, many service calls and state units.

evidence.text: Through it, daytime minutes take a typical customer steadily from under 1% at 112 to about 17% at 249 minutes, and an international plan from about 1% to about 16%; a voice-mail plan lowers the chance to under 1%.
The state moves it from about 1% in most other states to about 6% in California and about 5% in Washington, and to under 1% in Hawaii and Vermont.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.

hypothesis.text: This part adds up most inputs with fixed weights: daytime minutes, an international plan and voice-mail messages raise the chance of leaving, steadily for the minutes and messages, and a voice-mail plan lowers it.

evidence.text: It acts on 3147 of 4000 training customers, 409 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, it changes the chance by less than a point.

Through it, a typical customer's chance falls in an uneven way from about 47% at 91 minutes of daytime use to about 1% at 352 minutes, with no further fall past about 169 minutes (between 154 and 214 minutes for different customers).
A higher international charge lowers it only while it stays below about 2.96 US dollars (between 2.96 and 4.53 US dollars for different customers), in an uneven way, from about 4% to about 1%.

Customer-service calls raise it in an uneven way, from about 1% to about 3% between 0 and 3 calls, and from about 1% to about 6% with an evening charge of 17.12 US dollars or less, against no change above it.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.

hypothesis.text: This part raises the chance of leaving for customers with low usage, more so when they call customer service: daytime minutes lower it only while they stay below about 169 minutes (between 154 and 214 minutes for different customers), and calls raise it, both in an uneven way.

evidence.text: It acts on 306 of 4000 training customers, 154 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 16% without it and about 26% with it.
It is switched off in West Virginia: for the typical customer it acts on, being in any other state takes the chance from about 16% to about 26%.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.

hypothesis.text: This part raises the chance of leaving steadily with every call to customer service, from the first call on, except in West Virginia.

evidence.text: Through it, a voice-mail plan lowers a typical customer's chance by less than a point, and customers in states other than Alabama, North Carolina and West Virginia get about 2% instead of about 1%.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.

hypothesis.text: This part gives customers with a voice-mail plan a small discount on the chance of leaving.

evidence.text: Through it, a typical customer's chance moves by less than a point: about 2% in Tennessee and Ohio, and about 1% in Nevada and California.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.

hypothesis.text: This part adds small state offsets: up in Tennessee and Ohio, down in Nevada and California.

evidence.text: It is made up of these five parts (each explained below); the score is their sum, which was checked on all 4000 training customers.

Changing one input at a time across the whole model, an international plan takes a typical customer's chance of leaving from about 1% to about 16%, and more voice-mail messages raise it steadily, from about 1% at 0 to about 6% at 32 messages.
The model ignores the daytime charge, evening calls, international calls and the night-time charge.

hypothesis.text: The model adds up five parts into one score: fixed-weight inputs, calls with low usage, a voice-mail discount, many service calls and state units.

parts.name: csc_usage_gate
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis: a low-usage hinge whose threshold rises with customer service calls (CSC). 807 = relu(-1.36 dayMin + 0.05 CSC + 0.69*2627 + 0.61*2796 - 1.30), where 2627 = 1.01 + 0.32 relu(0.87 CSC - 0.09) (always positive, affine in a CSC hinge) and 2796 = relu(0.41 - 1.00 eveCharge + 0.37 CSC + 0.15 state:41 + 0.34*12926), with 12926/13061 a two-stage CSC hinge that turns on at 3 calls. 1264 = relu(0.077 - 0.32 intlCharge + 0.39*807) adds 0.39*807 and a convex low-intl-charge hinge. Readout 1.59*807 + 1.81*1264 (252 is near dead, readout -2e-5, and holds a state:2/state:44/state:4 path). Evidence (train, n=4000): sensitivity of 807 is dayMin 0.63, eveCharge 0.22, CSC 0.20. Mean gate logit rises 1.1 -> 7.4 from 0 to 7 calls. With the backbone +2.02 dayMin, the logit is V-shaped in day minutes; for CSC>=4 the low-usage arm dominates (empirical churn 0.88 low-day vs 0.24 high-day, which the network reproduces). The same hinge also lifts low-CSC, very-low-day customers (93 rows, predicted 0.17 vs empirical 0.04): a mild overextension. totalEveCharge equals totalEveMinutes after z-scoring, so the gate effectively uses evening usage. Ablation: linearising this gate drops train AUC 0.901 -> 0.851; restoring it alone on the fully linearised model gives 0.836 -> 0.899. It is the source of nearly all of the network s gain over a linear model.

parts.name: state_offsets
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis: per-state logit offsets. Every unit reads one (or a few) state one-hots, so it is an exact function of binary inputs and hence a constant offset per state: 10249 (state:3, -0.009 readout), 11427 (state:42, +0.05), 14942 (state:35, +0.04), 161_a (state:4, -0.03), 6730 (constant +0.43 logit except state:33, where it switches off: -0.45 logit for 77 rows), 8896 (state:19, <0.001), 3861 (state:50, dead on all rows). Evidence: sensitivity analysis on train; linear fit R2 = 1.0; zeroing all of them leaves AUC unchanged (0.9009). The state:33 switch has the opposite sign to the data (empirical log-odds +0.33).

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients
